name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,848

clue.text: National survey over the telephone

indicators.note: Down a phone line you get the sound of a word and not its spelling, so what is wanted is what the word sounds like.

blocks.note: A survey of opinion is a poll, and the two spellings are said exactly alike.

explanation.surface: Running a nationwide opinion survey by telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National' sits where an adjective describing the survey belongs and is a noun for a person from Poland. Polling by telephone is the picture the whole clue paints.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pole is a national of Poland — 'national' in the sense of a citizen of a country, not something nationwide.

clue.text: Old enough for starters to purchase cigarette?

definitions.text: Old enough for starters to purchase cigarette?

indicators.note: For starters means to begin with, so only the letters the words begin with are taken.
Purchase is the hold you get on a thing, so the letters already found take hold of what follows and close round it.

blocks.note: The letters OLD and ENOUGH start with, which then part to let the next chunk in.
A fag is British slang for a cigarette.

explanation.surface: Someone finally old enough to buy their own cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate definition to hunt for: the sentence builds the answer and describes it at the same time. 'For starters' reads as 'to begin with' in the surface and names initial letters in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of age is being old enough to buy your own cigarettes, so the sentence describes the answer as it stands, question mark and all.

clue.text: Ability to cope with nude swimming managed today

indicators.note: Letters set swimming are adrift from their moorings, and they wash up in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
Whoever ran the company managed it.
CE is Common Era, the dating label used today in place of AD.

explanation.surface: Someone who has managed a nude swim today.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, Common Era, is what modern scholarship writes where older books put AD, which is how one word of the surface comes down to two letters. 'Managed' is the boardroom sense, running a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to keep going under strain, which is the ability to cope with whatever is thrown at you.

clue.text: Holds frame for glasses masking grave expression

indicators.note: A frame runs round the outside of a thing, so only the outermost letters of the word named are taken.
To mask something is to cover it over, so what follows goes inside the letters already found.

blocks.note: The outside pair of letters of GLASSES, which then part company.
R.I.P., rest in peace, is the expression cut into a gravestone.

explanation.surface: Spectacle frames hiding a solemn look on someone's face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave expression' is not a look on anyone's face but the three letters carved on a headstone. R.I.P. stands for rest in peace and is one of the crossword's steadiest fillers.
explanation.definitionFit: To grip something is to hold it fast, and the definition matches the answer as the same verb in the third person.

clue.text: Exposed medium with two guardian spirits

indicators.note: Something exposed has had its covering stripped off, so the word named loses the letter at each end.

blocks.note: A medium is the agent through which something is brought about, and the A and the T at its ends come off.
Two in Roman numerals.

explanation.surface: A medium unmasked, along with a pair of protective spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium' is the seance sort in the surface and the means-to-an-end sort in the wordplay. The Romans gave every person and every place its own guardian, and this is the plural of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Genii is the plural of genius in its Roman sense: the attendant spirit given to a person or a place to look after it.

clue.text: Teeing off over par ultimately getting whole number

indicators.note: Something that has gone off is no longer as it was, so the letters named will not stay in their given order.
In a down clue, one chunk placed over another sits above it in the grid.
Ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word is wanted.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
The last letter of PAR.

explanation.surface: A golfer driving off the tee and finishing above par.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' does two jobs at once: it makes the golfing phrase in the surface and orders the shuffle in the wordplay. 'Over' is positional here, stacking one chunk above the other down the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: An integer is a number with nothing after the decimal point — a whole number.

clue.text: Write up further thoughts on adult resort

indicators.note: To write something up in a down clue is to set it climbing towards the top, so its letters come out back to front.

blocks.note: The further thoughts added after a letter is signed are its PS, the postscript.
A is the old film certificate for adult.

explanation.surface: Adding an afterthought about an adults-only holiday destination.
explanation.walkthrough: PS is what you write once you have already signed off, which is why 'further thoughts' translates into two letters. The turn is invisible until you notice this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a resort built round mineral springs, where people go to take the waters and be restored.

clue.text: Pressure fool to make the grade

blocks.note: P is pressure in the physics equations, alongside V for volume and T for temperature.
An ass is a fool, the donkey sitting behind the insult.

explanation.surface: Leaning on an idiot until he succeeds at something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure' reads as bullying and is a one-letter abbreviation from science. The definition is all three words, not just 'grade'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass an exam is to reach the required standard, which is what making the grade means.

clue.text: Still in bed retiring for present

indicators.note: To retire is to withdraw, to go back the way you came, so the letters named are read backwards.

blocks.note: Someone still in bed is not up, and that is the phrase before it is turned round.

explanation.surface: Someone who has gone back to bed rather than face the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' is the joke of the clue: it means going to bed in the surface and turning about-face in the wordplay. The five letters of the sleeper's excuse come back in a different order entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre puts on a play — presents it to an audience — so the two verbs swap directly.

clue.text: Obstruct nasty snot that's disgusting everyone

indicators.note: Something nasty has gone bad, and letters gone bad no longer sit in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
EW is the noise of disgust written down.
All means everyone, every last one of them.

explanation.surface: A revolting bit of snot that turns everybody's stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty' looks like a second adjective for the snot and is the instruction to disturb it. EW arrived in crosswords late and setters now use it as freely as ugh.
explanation.definitionFit: To stonewall is to block and delay rather than answer, the word used of a minister dodging questions or a batter refusing to score.

clue.text: First ever to mix up I and me

indicators.note: To mix things up is to jumble them together, so the letters named are stirred into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: The first person ever to confuse the two forms of the first-person pronoun.
explanation.walkthrough: Muddling 'I' and 'me' is a real thing people do, which is what lets the fodder sit in plain sight as a grammar complaint. The definition is the adjective used of a voyage, a flight or a batter's first century.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden voyage or a maiden flight is the first ever made, the adjective meaning never done before.

clue.text: Performing group stops complicated intro gaining popularity

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so the chunk named fills itself into the middle of the letters around it.
Something complicated has been tangled out of its plain order, so its letters need untangling into another.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters, which comes out as the frame the next chunk sits inside
An act is a performing group, the turn billed at a variety show.

explanation.surface: A band cutting into a convoluted introduction that is catching on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' is not halting anything: to stop a gap is to fill it. The definition is business jargon borrowed from tyres, where grip on the road became grip on the public.
explanation.definitionFit: Traction is the hold an idea gets on its audience: a campaign getting traction is one winning popularity.

clue.text: Focus of Ferrari to eavesdrop about new aerodynamic part

indicators.note: The focus of a thing is its centre point, so the middle letter of the word named is the one taken.
Something set about another thing is wrapped round it, so these letters close over the chunk that follows.

blocks.note: FERRARI has seven letters and the fourth, its middle one, is R.
To earwig is British slang for listening in on other people's conversations.
N is the standard abbreviation for new.

explanation.surface: Ferrari concentrating on listening in for news of a rival's aerodynamics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earwig' as a verb means to listen in, a British colloquialism with nothing to do with the insect. 'Focus of Ferrari' looks like the team's priority and asks instead for the centre of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rear wing is the aerofoil mounted across the back of a racing car to press its tyres down on the track.

clue.text: Who attempts to get in touch with twin?

definitions.text: Who attempts to get in touch

blocks.clueFragment: Who attempts to get in touch
blocks.note: The one making the phone call.
The second sense of the same word: a double close enough to be passed off as the original.

explanation.surface: Asking who is trying to reach one of a pair of twins.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on the same verb: placing a telephone call, and the old racing sense of a horse substituted for another to fool the bookmakers. The question mark covers the stretch from double to twin.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the person at the other end of the telephone call; the other is the dead ringer, a double so close it could pass for the original.

clue.text: Cobra certainly eclipses North American snake

indicators.note: To eclipse something is to pass across it and cover it up, so what is wanted lies hidden under the words named.

blocks.note: The letters run straight on across the gap, from the fourth letter of COBRA into CERTAINLY.

explanation.surface: One snake definitely overshadowing another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eclipses' covers in the wordplay and outshines in the surface, which is how one snake comes to hide inside the name of another. Colubrids of this kind move at close to ten miles an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: The racer is a long, slender, fast-moving snake of North America, the black racer being the familiar one.

clue.text: Outing secret agent finishing early at work

indicators.note: A word that finishes early stops before its last letter, which therefore never arrives.

blocks.note: A secret agent is a spy, and it is the Y that is dropped.
Someone at work is in, as against out of the office.

explanation.surface: A spy knocking off before the end of his shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outing' next to a secret agent reads as exposing him, and means a drive in the country. 'In' for at work is the office sense, the word on the board beside your name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin is a short outing in a car, as in going out for a spin on a Sunday afternoon.

clue.text: An effort to support green vegetables in farming class

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever supports something sits underneath it, so these letters go below the ones clued next.

blocks.note: Peas are the green vegetables, and they take the top of a down clue.
Lifted straight from the clue.
A try is an effort, as in giving something a try.

explanation.surface: Making an effort on behalf of greens grown on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' is positional rather than political: in a down clue the supporting chunk goes underneath. The class the definition names is the bottom rung of the feudal order, working land they did not own.
explanation.definitionFit: The peasantry are the class of smallholders and farm labourers who live off the land they work.

clue.text: Concerned with design of street away from the town crossing defaced channel

indicators.note: One thing crossing another cuts through the middle of it, so the letters named land inside.
A word defaced has lost its face, the letter at its front.

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation on every street sign and envelope.
Country areas away from the town are rural, and the word opens after its first letter.
A channel is a duct, here with its opening D struck off.

explanation.surface: A road layout out in the country, crossing a vandalised waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away from the town' is a full definition of a word buried in the wordplay rather than a piece of the surface geography. 'Defaced' is meant literally — a word losing its face loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Structural questions are the ones about how a thing is put together rather than how it looks, which is design in the engineer's sense.

clue.text: Hurry son and daughter outside to go to the toilet

indicators.note: Standing outside something means being on either side of it, so these letters close round the chunk named next.

blocks.note: S is son, the abbreviation used in family trees and Who's Who entries.
The nursery verb for going to the toilet.
D is daughter, its partner in the same family-tree shorthand.

explanation.surface: Two children waiting outside while somebody uses the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' is where the children stand in the surface and the wrapping instruction in the wordplay. S and D are family-tree abbreviations that crosswords lean on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: To speed is to hurry, to move faster than is strictly allowed.

clue.text: Peacekeepers try to work out fine lacking precedent

blocks.note: The United Nations supply the blue-helmeted peacekeeping forces.
A court hears a case, which is how a case gets tried.
To do a sum or a puzzle is to work it out.
F is the pencil grade for fine, stamped on the barrel beside HB.

explanation.surface: Peacekeeping troops trying to calculate a penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' is the courtroom verb, and to try a case is to hear it. F for fine comes off the side of a pencil, where it sits with HB and B.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unheard-of has never happened before, so there is no precedent for it.

clue.text: One leading expert's entertained by favourite theory regularly

indicators.note: A host entertaining a guest has them in the house, so the chunk named goes inside the one doing the entertaining.
Taking letters regularly means taking them at even intervals, every other one, rather than in a run.

blocks.note: A favourite is a pet, as in a pet subject, and the word opens after its first letter.
An expert is an ace, and the apostrophe-s of the surface hands over the S.
The first, third and fifth letters of THEORY.

explanation.surface: A top expert being made much of on the strength of a favourite theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Favourite theory' sits together like the pet theory it is pretending to be, and the clue prises the two words apart to use them separately. 'Regularly' here takes the odd letters, starting from the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacesetter is the runner out in front dictating the speed for the field behind, so the one leading is exactly what it names.

clue.text: I'm hesitant to enter line of vehicles making ground

indicators.note: To enter something is to go inside it, so these letters are planted within the word named next.

blocks.note: A line of vehicles coupled together is a train, which opens after its first letter.
ER is the noise I make when I am hesitating.

explanation.surface: Someone dithering before joining a queue of traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm hesitant' wants the little noise itself rather than a word meaning hesitant, which is why two letters answer four words. The definition is the surveyor's and the soldier's word for the lie of the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrain is ground considered as a stretch of country — what soldiers and walkers mean by the lie of the land.

clue.text: Glory hole's opening next to a toilet wiping rear

indicators.note: The opening of a word is the letter it starts with, so only that one is taken.
Wiping the rear of a word rubs out the letter at the end of it.

blocks.note: The letter HOLE begins with.
Taken straight from the clue.
A loo is a toilet, and the second O is rubbed off the end.

explanation.surface: The door of a junk cupboard beside the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: A glory hole is the British name for the cluttered cupboard under the stairs, so the first two words look like one thing and are two. 'Glory' on its own belongs to religious art.
explanation.definitionFit: Glory is the term religious painters use for the ring of light round a saint's head, which is what the answer is.

clue.text: Californian law enforcement arresting perp not half drunk

indicators.note: Arresting someone means taking them in, so the chunk named is held inside the letters around it.
A word that is not half is only half, and here it is the front half that stays.

blocks.note: The LAPD is the Los Angeles Police Department, Los Angeles being in California, and it opens after its third letter.
Half of PERP, American police shorthand for the perpetrator of a crime.

explanation.surface: Los Angeles police cuffing a suspect who is half cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' ends the clue looking like the state of the suspect and is the past participle of drink. The two American police terms carry each other's surface, which is what hides the split.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat that has lapped its saucer has drunk it, 'lapped' being the past participle of drinking with the tongue.

clue.text: Cool writer captures lives

indicators.note: To capture something is to take it prisoner, so the chunk named is shut inside the letters around it.

blocks.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the writer crosswords reach for when three letters are wanted, opening after its second.
He lives is he is, the same verb in the third person.

explanation.surface: A calm author capturing people's lives on the page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives' looks like biography material and is the verb to be. 'Cool' as a noun, the thing you keep or lose, does the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Poise is composure under pressure — cool in the sense of keeping yours when everyone else is losing theirs.

clue.text: The man on seat secures coach

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast, so what is held ends up inside the letters that hold it.

blocks.note: Re means on the subject of, as at the head of a memo.
The blunt British word for the backside you sit on.
The man is he, and he goes between the two chunks above.

explanation.surface: A man in his seat making a coach safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' is anatomical here, the part of you that meets the chair. 'Coach' looks like the vehicle the seat belongs to and is a verb instead, while 'on' is doing the memo-heading job.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehearse a cast is to take them through the piece again and again, which is the job the verb 'coach' names.

clue.text: Free type of takeaway's set aside cold

definitions.note: 'Free' is an adjective and the answer a noun; the setter names the type by the single quality that defines it, free of convention and free of possessions.

indicators.note: To set something aside is to put it out of the way, so the letter named next is left out.

blocks.note: A chippy is the British fish-and-chip shop, the oldest sort of takeaway.
Cold is C, the letter on the tap, and that is what gets set aside.

explanation.surface: A chip shop putting something cold to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive in the surface and means 'has' in the wordplay, which is what lets a shop set a letter aside. C for cold comes off the taps.
explanation.definitionFit: A hippy is defined by living free of convention — free love, free festivals, free of a job — so the adjective stands in for the person.

clue.text: Sit semi-naked in this sweater?

blocks.note: The surface offers a woolly jumper, with the odd picture of somebody sitting half-dressed inside it.
The setter means a thing that makes you sweat, not a thing you pull over your head.

explanation.surface: Sitting half-dressed inside a woolly jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the pun: 'sweater' is read as sweat-er, an agent noun coined on the spot. Half-dressed is exactly how you are dressed for the thing the setter means.
explanation.definitionFit: A sauna is the hot wooden room you sit in wearing a towel and nothing else, and it makes you sweat, which is the whole of the joke.

clue.text: I hope it breaks American nation

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart, and the pieces go back together in another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
A is the abbreviation for American, as in the A of the USA.

explanation.surface: Wishing damage on a country somewhere in the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American nation' looks like one phrase and is two jobs: A does the abbreviating and 'nation' the defining. The country that comes out is on the wrong continent entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethiopia is a country of the Horn of Africa, so the definition places the answer by category and nothing else.

clue.text: Dirty place arises where antiperspirant may be required

indicators.note: What arises comes up, and in a down clue letters coming up the grid are read from the bottom.

blocks.note: A tip is the British municipal rubbish dump, and any filthy room gets called one too.

explanation.surface: A squalid dump coming up where the smell would call for deodorant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' in British use covers both the council dump and a bedroom in a state, which is why 'dirty place' is enough to pin it. The definition takes the long way round to a word of three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Armpit is shortened to pit in everyday speech, and the armpit is where a deodorant goes.

clue.text: Stage cricket match for all ages in afternoon

indicators.note: 'In' puts what has just been clued inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: Afternoon is p.m., and the two letters part company.
An ODI is a one-day international, the fifty-over form of the game.
U is the British film certificate for a film anybody of any age may watch.

explanation.surface: A cricket match played in the afternoon and fit for the whole family.
explanation.walkthrough: Both abbreviations are British institutions: the one-day international out of the cricket pages, and the U certificate off a children's film poster. 'Stage' is the noun, not the verb the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: A podium is the small raised stage a conductor, a speaker or a medallist stands on.

clue.text: Part of car exhaust heard

indicators.note: What is heard is a sound, so the word wanted is the one that sounds like the word given.

blocks.note: To exhaust somebody is to tire them, and the British spelling of the car part differs by a letter.

explanation.surface: Listening to a car's exhaust note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust' is planted next to 'car' so that it reads as the pipe, and it is the verb meaning to wear out. British spelling puts a Y where American spelling keeps an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre is the rubber hoop fitted round a car's wheel, so the definition names it by where it belongs.

clue.text: Brown crust of gooseberry tart

indicators.note: A crust is the outside of a thing, so the word named gives up only its outermost letters.

blocks.note: Tan is a shade of brown.
The outside pair of letters of GOOSEBERRY.

explanation.surface: The browned crust of a gooseberry tart.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the pudding is doing another job: 'crust of' is an instruction and 'tart' the definition. Gooseberries are sharp enough to need burying in sugar, which is what holds the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tart of a food means sharp enough to make you screw your face up, which is what tangy describes.

clue.text: Attempt to draw attention of two females as the second turns around

indicators.note: Something that turns around ends up facing the other way, so its letters are read back to front.

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female, and this is the first of the two.
The second female is a gal, and she is the one that turns.

explanation.surface: Trying to catch the eye of two women, one of whom turns round.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second of the two females reverses, which is what 'the second' is there to tell you. GAL is the informal girl crosswords fall back on when three letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag a taxi, or to flag an item for someone's notice, is to try to catch attention by waving something.
